---
title: Mallard Duck Movement
author: Angela Davaadorj
execute:
  echo: false
---

Mallard ducks are a familiar and widely distributed species of dabbling duck, known for their adaptability, strong seasonal movement, and use of wetlands, lakes, and agricultural areas. Their movements are shaped by breeding, migration, and changing food availability, making them a useful species for studying how animals respond to environmental change.

Lake Constance, located on the border of Germany, Switzerland, and Austria, is an important wetland region for many migratory birds. It provides a rich stopover and wintering area where ducks can rest, forage, and move across a broad landscape. The lake and surrounding lowlands are a natural setting for tracking how individual birds move through the region over time.

The GPS tracking data used here records the movements of individual Mallards across multiple years. By examining the timing, distribution, and seasonal patterns in the locations, we can see how different birds use the region and how their routes change across the annual cycle. These tracks reveal both the shared migration context and the unique movement behavior of each duck.

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
```

```{r}
#| cache: true
mallards <- readRDS("data/mallards.rds")
```

```{r}
fix_counts <- mallards |>
  count(duck_id, sort = TRUE)

fix_counts
```

```{r}
range_summary <- mallards |>
  summarise(
    min_lat = min(lat, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_lat = max(lat, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_lon = min(long, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_lon = max(long, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

range_summary
```
